tales.title: The lake took my brother's canoe
text: Two springs ago my brother and I went out on the big lake in a bark canoe to set nets for whitefish. The lake was flat as a dish when we left. By noon it was a wall of grey water, higher than a lodge, and the wind came out of the north-east like a fist.

We turned for the shore and the waves threw us onto the sandbar at the river mouth. The canoe broke in two. My brother could not swim well, and I held him by the hair until our feet found sand. We walked home soaked, with no fish and no canoe, and our mother laughed until she cried and then cried until she laughed. The lake is not a river. It does not care who you are. Never trust it on a calm morning.

tales.title: Trading with the Sauk
text: Every few summers I go west to the Rock River to trade with the Sauk. They have horses from the far plains and lead from the mines near the Mississippi, and we have goods from the traders here at the lake. One of their war leaders there is a hard man called Black Hawk, who hates the Americans almost as much as Main Poc does.

He told me the Americans took the Sauk land along the Mississippi with a treaty that his people never agreed to, signed by men who were drunk and had no right. He says he will never forgive it. I believe him. I have never met a man who held a grudge so carefully, like a coal kept alive in a shell. One day, I think, that coal will set the prairie burning.

tales.title: How I got my name
text: When I was a baby my grandfather gave me my name. He had a dream, and in the dream he saw what my name should be, and he stood up at the naming feast and said it out loud four times so that the spirits would hear it. Then everyone said it with him, and I was a person.

The soldiers cannot say my name. They call me by some word that sounds a little like it, or by the colour of my blanket, or they do not call me anything. A man without a name to his neighbours is a stranger to them. It is easy to fear a stranger. It is easy to hurt one.

tales.title: Forty brooches for a winter
text: Last spring I came in from the winter grounds with a good pack: forty muskrat, twelve otter, a bear hide, a bale of deer skins. I took it all to the trader with the big house. I paid my debt for the powder and the blanket, and I had enough left for forty silver brooches for my wife.

The trader made them himself at his bench while I watched, beating the silver thin and cutting the holes with a little chisel. He makes them better than anyone. He asked after my wife by name. That is why we trade with him and not the government store. A man who knows your wife's name is not only a trader. Find him if you want to see the silver.

tales.title: The river of the wild onion
text: The river here is called after the wild onion, or the skunk, depending on who tells it: the plant that grows thick in the wet ground along the banks and smells strong when you crush it. The French wrote the name down as best they could, and the Americans write it the way the French did.

It is a poor little river. Slow and muddy and almost nothing in summer. But it is the door between the great lake and the great river to the west, and so every people who ever wanted to go anywhere has come through it. That is why there is a fort here. That is why there are so many of us here this week. Doors are where people quarrel.

tales.title: The last elk on the prairie
text: When I was a boy there were elk on the prairie west of here, big herds of them, and buffalo too, some years. I saw my first buffalo when I was eight, a whole dark river of them flowing across the grass at the far edge of the sky.

Now the elk are few and the buffalo do not come this far east any more. The hunters say the guns have frightened them away, or the fires, or the fort. My son has never seen a buffalo. I have told him what they look like. He thinks I am making it up, the way old men do.

tales.title: My son wants to see the soldiers
text: My son is ten and he wants to go to the fort every day to watch the soldiers march. He stands at the edge of the parade with his friends and copies them, stiff-legged, with a stick on his shoulder, and the soldiers laugh and the sergeant shouts at them to stop laughing.

This week I have forbidden him to go. He asked me why, and I did not have a good answer. I told him the soldiers are busy. He said the soldiers are always busy. He is right. I am a coward in front of my own son. How do you tell a boy that his friends may be his enemies tomorrow?

tales.title: I heard Tecumseh speak
text: Two summers ago Tecumseh came to our village and spoke at the council fire. He is not a tall man, but when he speaks you cannot look anywhere else. He said the red people are one people, from the lakes to the gulf, and that the land belongs to all of us together, and that no chief may sell any of it without the consent of all.

He said: the white people are like a flood. One drop at a time it does not seem like much. But if every nation stands alone, the flood will cover us one by one. Stand together and it cannot. I have thought about those words every day since. I think about them tonight more than ever.

tales.title: The man who mends guns
text: My gun is an English trade gun, the lock gone loose from a bad fall on the ice. In the spring I took it to the fort, because there is a sergeant there named Hays who is good with locks, and kind. He sat on the bank with me for an hour with his little tools and fixed it, and would take nothing for it but a pipe of tobacco.

I have thought about that sergeant all week. He did not need to help me. He did it because he is the kind of man who helps. In every people there are men like that, and they are always the ones who get hurt. If you see him, tell him the lock still holds.

tales.title: My wife sits in council too
text: The soldiers think only men decide things among us. They are wrong. The women decide who will be chief, among some of our families, and the women decide whether there will be food for a war party, and the women decide whether a captive will be adopted into a family or not.

Last night my wife sat with the other women of our lodges for a long time, and when she came back she told me what they had decided. I will not tell you what it was. But I will tell you that I listened. A man who does not listen to his wife in a week like this is a man who will be sorry.

tales.title: The men from the Wabash
text: Some of the men who have come in this week are from the Wabash, from the Prophet's people, and they are different from us. They do not trade with Kinzie. They do not know the soldiers by name. They have no friends inside those walls, only enemies.

When they speak at the fires, the young men of our own villages listen to them like children to a storyteller. Our chiefs say, these soldiers are our neighbours. The Wabash men say, these soldiers are the ones who burned our town. Both are telling the truth. It is the second truth that is louder.

tales.title: The goods from the store
text: Today the soldiers gave out the goods from the government store: cloth, blankets, kettles, paint, tobacco. People carried them away to their lodges. I took a blanket for my mother, a good red one.

But the guns were not given out, or the powder, or the whiskey. The captain promised them at the council two days ago, I was there and heard it. And now they say the guns are broken and in the well and the whiskey is in the river. My mother says a blanket is a blanket and to be glad of it. My mother is wiser than the young men. But I am one of the young men.

tales.title: The road from Milwaukee
text: I came down from Milwaukee three days ago with a party of twenty, along the lake shore trail. At every creek we met others going the same way, from the north and the west, families with their horses and dogs and kettles, all walking toward Chicago.

It was like the whole country was moving, like birds before a storm. Nobody had told us to come. We came because everybody was coming. That is how great things happen, I think. Not because a chief says so. Because everybody starts walking in the same direction at once and nobody can stop.

tales.title: The interpreter who was killed
text: The interpreter, Lalime, was a quiet man and a fair one. When we went to the fort to speak to the captain, he put our words into English carefully, without adding or taking away. Not every interpreter does that.

Then in June the trader Kinzie killed him at the gate, and the soldiers did nothing. Kinzie went away for a while and came back, and now he sits on his porch looking at Lalime's grave. I am not saying Kinzie was in the wrong. Nobody knows what happened between them. I am saying that a fort where a man can kill the interpreter and walk free is not a place that keeps its own laws. Why would it keep its word to us?

tales.title: My uncle's advice
text: My uncle took me aside last night. He is an old man and he has fought in more wars than I have years. He said: when it starts, and it will start, do not be the first to run forward, and do not be the last to stay. The first are killed and the last are disgraced. Be in the middle.
Then he said: and when it is over, remember that you will have to live with what you did for the rest of your life. Do only what you can live with. Then he went to sleep. I have not slept at all.

tales.title: A winter of muskrats
text: Muskrats live in the marshes in little houses of reeds and mud, like tiny lodges. In winter, when the ice is thick, you walk out on the marsh and break into their houses with a spear, very quietly, and catch them inside. Their fur is soft and the traders like it, and their meat is good to eat.

Last winter I took two hundred. My fingers froze so badly I could not close my hand for a week. My wife rubbed them with fat and scolded me for being greedy. I said I was not greedy, I was in debt. She said those were the same thing with the traders. She is right about most things.

tales.title: My dog knows
text: My dog has been strange all week. She growls at the soldiers when they come near the river, which she never did before. She will not leave my side at night. She looks toward the fort and whines.

The old people say dogs can see what is coming before men can. I do not know if that is true. But I know my dog is not a fool, and she has decided something. I scratched her ears tonight and told her she was a good dog. She looked at me as if she wanted to tell me something, and could not. I know the feeling.

tales.title: From Black Partridge's village
text: I am from Black Partridge's village on the Illinois River, across from the head of Peoria Lake. He is a good chief. He has kept the peace with the Americans for seventeen years and he has kept us out of every war that came near.

This week he has been sitting with the other chiefs from morning until night, and when he comes back to our fire he does not speak. Last night I saw him take off his American medal and hold it in his hand for a long time, looking at it. Then he put it back on. Go and see him if you can. You will understand what kind of man he is when you look at his face.

tales.title: The scout's reputation
text: Everyone in this camp knows the name of Wells. When the Americans' armies came into our country twenty years ago, Wells was scouting for them. He knew where our villages were, and how we fought, because he had been one of the Miami himself. Many of our people died because of what he knew.

So when he rode in yesterday with his Miami, some of the young men spat on the ground. Some of the older men nodded to him, because they remember him from before, when he was Little Turtle's son-in-law and the Americans' enemy. A man with two lives has two kinds of enemies. Wells has more than anyone.

tales.title: My ball stick
text: This is my ball stick. I made it from a hickory sapling three summers ago, bent while it was green and tied until it set, with a net of rawhide at the end. It has played in nine great games. I have won six.

I will not play with it this summer. There is a different game coming, and it is played with different sticks. But I am going to keep it beside me tonight anyway, for luck. A man needs something from the old days in his hand on a night like this.

tales.title: A dress for my daughter
text: I have been sewing a dress for my daughter all summer, of red stroud from the trader, with ribbon at the hem and twenty brooches across the shoulders. She will wear it at the dances in the fall when the people come in from the hunting grounds, and the young men will look at her.

Tonight I finished the last brooch. She tried it on by the fire and turned round and round, and the brooches chimed. She is so beautiful. I did not tell her what I was afraid of. I told her the young men had better watch out. She laughed. I want to remember that laugh for the rest of my life.

tales.title: Wild rice in the north
text: My mother came from the north, near the Menominee country, where the wild rice grows in the shallow lakes. In the fall the women go out in canoes, two to a boat, one pushing with a pole and one bending the stalks over and knocking the grains in with sticks. Then you parch it over a fire and dance on it to loosen the husks.

There is no wild rice here at the river. It is too muddy, and the water is wrong. My mother missed it every fall. She used to say a woman without wild rice in her stores was a poor woman, however rich her husband. I never ate it until I was grown. Now I would give anything for one bowl.

tales.title: The trader's wife
text: The trader's wife, Mrs. Kinzie, speaks some of the languages of the eastern nations, because she lived among the Senecas when she was a little girl. They took her from her family and adopted her, and she loved them, and when her people came to take her back she cried.

So she is not like the other American women. She looks at us as if we are people. She has eaten in my lodge, and I have eaten in her house, and her daughter Margaret used to run in and out of our camp when she was small. Find her if you can. She will treat you kindly, whoever you are. That is how she is.

tales.title: Too many horses
text: There are so many horses in this camp now that the grass is eaten down to the dirt for a mile in every direction. My boys take ours farther out each day to find grazing, and come back later each night. I worry about them out on the prairie in the dark.

Everything is too much this week. Too many people, too many horses, too many fires, too much talking. Not enough food, not enough grass, not enough sleep. When a place has too much of the wrong things and not enough of the right ones, something has to break. I only hope it breaks gently.

tales.title: The cradle board
text: My baby rides on my back in a cradle board, laced in snug with moss under him to keep him dry. His grandfather carved the board and the hoop over his face, so if I drop him the hoop takes the blow. From the hoop hang little things to watch: a shell, a carved bird, a string of beads.

He watches the whole world from up there, over my shoulder, and never cries. The soldiers' wives think it is cruel to lace a baby so tight. I think it is cruel to let a baby kick and scream on the floor, as they do. Each people thinks the other people raises children wrong. Every mother is sure.

tales.title: My sister married a Frenchman in the fort
text: My sister married one of the Frenchmen who works for the trader, years ago, and she lives in his log house on the north bank with their children. When the settlers ran into the fort in April, she went with them, because her husband did.

So now my sister is inside the walls and I am outside them. We stood on either side of the river this morning and waved to each other. She held up her youngest so I could see how big he has grown. I wanted to shout across to her, come out, come home. I did not. She has made her choice. I pray it is the right one.

tales.title: An old woman's work
text: I am old, and old women have a special work: we remember. We remember who is related to whom, and which family owes which, and who was born in which winter. When the young people forget, they come to us.

And we have another work, which nobody speaks of. When there is fighting, it is the old women who decide what happens afterwards. Who is adopted. Who is spared. Who is sent home. The men think they make the war. They do. But we make the peace that comes after. Remember that, if anyone tells you the women have no power here.

tales.title: Quills before ribbons
text: Before the traders brought ribbon, my grandmother decorated everything with porcupine quills. You soften them in your mouth, flatten them with your teeth, dye them with roots and berries, and sew them down in patterns so fine you would think they were painted.

I still do quillwork on moccasins for my family, though it takes ten times as long as ribbon. My daughter says why bother, when the trader has ribbon in every colour. I tell her: because your grandmother's hands taught mine, and mine will teach yours, and when you sew quills you are holding her hands. She rolls her eyes. One day she will understand.

tales.title: I won the race
text: Today the boys of our camp raced the boys from the Milwaukee camp, all the way from the big oak to the river and back. I won. I ran so fast my feet hardly touched the grass, and the Milwaukee boy behind me fell in a muskrat hole.

My grandfather saw it and gave me a piece of dried meat as a prize, and said that when he was young he could run all day without stopping, from sunrise to sunset. My grandmother said he could not, he could only talk all day without stopping. Everybody laughed. It was the first time anybody laughed all week.

tales.title: The puppies
text: Our dog had five puppies in the spring, under the edge of the lodge. I got to name them all. One is called Little Thunder because he barks so loud, and one is called Mud because he is always muddy, and one is called Sleepy.

I wanted to give one to the boy in the fort, the one with the yellow hair. My mother said no, not this week. I asked her when. She said maybe in the fall. I am saving Sleepy for him. Sleepy is the nicest one.

tales.title: My grandmother's summer story
text: In summer my grandmother will not tell the real stories, only made-up ones. Tonight she told one about a raccoon who wanted to wash everything in the world, even the moon, and he waited by the lake every night until the moon came down to the water, and then he tried to wash it, and it broke into a hundred pieces.

Then he cried, because he thought he had broken the moon. But the next night it was whole again, up in the sky. Grandmother said: some things that look broken are only resting. Then she sent us to sleep. My little sister fell asleep right away. I lay awake thinking about the moon.

tales.title: My mother's dress
text: My mother finished my new dress today, red, with twenty silver brooches on the shoulders. When I turn round it rings like little bells. I am going to wear it at the dances in the fall.

I asked if I could wear it tomorrow, to show the other girls. My mother said no, very fast, in a strange voice. Then she hugged me too tight. I do not know why grown-ups are so strange this week. I put my dress away carefully with the brooches inside so they will not get scratched.

tales.title: My first bird
text: Today I shot my first bird with my little bow, a blackbird in the reeds by the river. My father made the bow from ash and the arrows from cane, and he has been teaching me since the spring snow.

I brought it to my mother and she cooked it in the fire and gave the first piece to my grandfather, because that is how it is done with a boy's first game. My grandfather ate it slowly and said it was the best meal of his life. I know it was only a blackbird. But I felt very tall.

tales.title: Our town at the three rivers
text: Our town is at Kekionga, where the St. Joseph and the St. Marys rivers join to make the Maumee. It was the greatest town of the Miami, with the cornfields stretching for miles. The Americans built Fort Wayne right beside it, after General Wayne beat us all at Fallen Timbers.

So we live beside a fort, as the Potawatomi do here. We know what it is like, to have soldiers for neighbours. Some days they are good neighbours and some days they are not. It depends on the captain, and on the news from the east, and on the whiskey. Mostly on the whiskey.

tales.title: Sweet Breeze
text: Wells married Little Turtle's daughter, Sweet Breeze, when he was still a Miami warrior. She bore him children, and she died young, years ago. Her children are Miami and they are American, both, like their father.

Wells sent his children to be schooled in Kentucky, but he keeps them close in his heart. On the road here he told me that his daughter had written him a letter in English with every word spelled wrong, and that he kept it in his coat. He showed it to me. I could not read it. But I could see how he held it.

tales.title: We are a tired people
text: The Miami fought the Americans for twenty years and won great battles, and lost, and lost again. Then at Greenville we made peace and promised to keep it, and we have. Our chief Little Turtle kept it even when the young men wanted war, even when Tecumseh came to our town and called him a coward.

Now Little Turtle is dead, a month ago, and the young men are restless again. I do not want war. I have buried a father and two brothers. I want to go home and plant corn and grow old. That is what I am riding here for: to bring these soldiers home so that maybe, just maybe, there will be one less war.

tales.title: The road along the lake
text: Tomorrow we go back the way we came, along the lake shore, then inland through the woods to Fort Wayne. It is a long road, through the sand and then through the swamps, and with wagons and women and children it will take many days.

Wells has put some of us in front of the column and some of us behind. I am in front. I would rather be in front. If something is going to happen, I want to see it coming. A man at the back hears it before he sees it, and that is worse.

tales.title: I can beat the drum
text: Hugh McPherson the drummer let me hold his sticks once, and I beat the call for dinner on an upturned bucket, and the whole company came running and found nothing in the kettle. I was in trouble for a week. It was worth it.

He says a drummer must count in his head all day, even when he is asleep, and that is why drummers are strange. He showed me the long roll, which goes brrrrrrrr, and he says it is only for very serious things. I asked him if he would play it tomorrow. He said he hoped not. Go and find him. If he is in a good mood he will show you the long roll too.

tales.title: The dancing birds
text: In the spring the big grey cranes come to the marsh behind the fort and dance. They jump up in the air and flap and bow to each other, like ladies at a ball, and they make a noise like a wooden rattle. My father says they are courting.

I sneaked out to watch them one morning in May, though we were not allowed past the gate after the killings at the farm. A soldier on the wall saw me and shouted, and the cranes flew away, and I got a whipping. But I saw them first. Nobody can take that away.

tales.title: Maple sugar in a bark box
text: John Kinzie, the big one, has a son called John too, who is nine, and he gets maple sugar whenever he wants it, in a box made of birch bark with a picture scratched on the lid. The Potawatomi women make it in the spring in the woods, boiling the sap for days.

John gave me a piece once. It tastes like the smell of a fire. He says his father is going to take them all away in the boat tomorrow and he is not frightened at all, and then he went very quiet. Find him and ask him for some sugar. He might give you a bit if you say please and do not tell his mother.

tales.title: Watching the drill
text: Every morning the soldiers march up and down the parade and the sergeant shouts at them, and they all turn at once like a fence falling over. I practise in the yard with a stick for a musket. I can do shoulder arms and present arms and right face. I cannot do left face, I always turn the wrong way.

When I am big I am going to be a sergeant, so I can shout. My mother says I already shout enough. Today the soldiers drilled for a long time, longer than ever, and nobody was laughing at all. I stopped practising and just watched.

tales.title: My friend in the camp
text: There is a boy in the camp across the river who is the same size as me. We cannot talk to each other but we can race. He always wins. He can swim like an otter and he can shoot a bird with a little bow, and he laughed when I fell in the river.

I gave him a brass button off my old coat and he gave me a feather with a red tip. I have it in my hat. This week my mother says I may not go near the river at all. I saw him on the other bank yesterday and waved, and he waved, and then a man called him away. I hope he keeps the button.

tales.title: The river smells funny
text: Last night the soldiers rolled all the barrels down to the river and broke them open. This morning the whole river smells like my father's breath on a holiday. The fish must be very confused.

The grown-ups are cross and quiet. A lady told me the men in the camps were angry because the whiskey was meant for them. I asked why soldiers would pour away something people wanted, and nobody answered me. I think when grown-ups do not answer it means the answer is frightening.

tales.title: We are going in the wagon
text: Tomorrow we are all going away to Fort Wayne, and the little children and the sick soldiers get to ride in the wagons. I am not little but my mother says I am to ride anyway. I wanted to walk with the soldiers. She said absolutely not in her not-arguing voice.

I have packed my feather and my knife and my wooden horse. My sister has packed her doll and three acorns. Mama has packed our Bible in her apron. We are going to walk along the lake shore all the way, she says, so I will see the lake all day. I like the lake. It is the biggest thing I know.

tales.title: Josette's stories
text: Josette who looks after the Kinzie children knows the best stories in the world. She tells one about a giant who walks across the lake in winter, so big that the ice cracks under him and that is why the ice makes noises. And one about a little bird that tricked a bear.

She says the old people only tell the real stories in winter when there is snow on the ground, because the spirits are sleeping then and will not be offended. In summer she tells made-up ones instead. Find her and ask for a summer story. She will pretend to be too busy and then tell you one anyway.

tales.title: I was born in Chicago
text: I was born here, in the fort, when the snow was on the ground. My mother says I was the first baby she ever saw come into the world in a blockhouse. I do not remember being born, obviously.

I have never seen a town. I have never seen a church, or a shop, or a brick, or a road that goes anywhere. My father says that in Ohio there are houses side by side for miles and they all have glass windows. I do not believe him. I think he is teasing me again.

tales.title: The fattest baby in the fort
text: Mrs. Burns had a baby in April, the night before we all ran into the fort, and they carried her across the river in her bed. Now the baby is the fattest baby in Chicago and it cries louder than the morning gun.

I help mind it sometimes. If you jiggle it and sing Yankee Doodle it stops crying for exactly as long as the song. Then it starts again. Mrs. Burns says I am very useful. Go and see the baby. It is very ugly and very nice.

tales.title: The bravest girl
text: Isabella Cooper is nine and she is not afraid of anything. She climbed up the flagpole halfway once and the sergeant had to get her down with a ladder. She can carry a full bucket from the river without spilling. She fights the boys and wins.

Her mother is Mrs. Burns, and her new father is the sergeant of the militia. Tonight Isabella told me that if anybody tries to hurt her mother tomorrow she will bite them. She means it. Go and find her. Do not get in a fight with her.

tales.title: The ball game
text: When the men play the ball game it goes on all afternoon, a hundred on each side, running across the prairie with their sticks, and the goals are so far apart you cannot see one from the other. The women bet their best things on it, kettles and blankets and silver, and shout louder than the players.

We boys play with little sticks and a ball of deer hair. My uncle made my stick from a hickory sapling, bent and tied while it was green, with a pocket of rawhide. I am the fastest in my lodge. This summer the men have not played. My uncle says there are other games coming. He did not smile when he said it.

tales.title: The boy in the fort
text: There is a boy in the fort who is my size, with hair the colour of dry grass. We race on the bank. I always win. He gave me a button, a shining one with a bird on it, and I gave him a feather.

My mother says I must not cross the river now. The grown-ups talk late into the night around the fire, and they send us children away so we cannot hear. I hear anyway. I keep the button in my pouch. I do not know if that is right or wrong now. I keep it anyway.

tales.title: The sugar camp
text: In the spring when the snow starts to go, we go to the maple woods, all the families together. The women cut the trees and set bark pans under them, and the sap drips all day, and we children carry it to the big kettles. When it boils down thick my grandmother pours some on the snow and it goes hard and we eat it.

That is the best time of the year. Everybody is happy and tired and sticky. My little brother ate so much he was sick, and my grandmother laughed and said that was how she knew he was a real boy. I would like it to be spring again.

tales.title: My first canoe
text: My father is making me a canoe of my own, a little one, from a single log burned and scraped hollow. He lets me scrape the burned part out with a shell. It is very slow. My father says patience is the first thing a canoe teaches you, before it teaches you to paddle.

When it is finished I will paddle it on the river and catch fish. I will paddle it out to the lake if my mother lets me, which she will not. My father says it will be ready before the leaves turn. Then he looked at the fort and said, if we are still here.

tales.title: Their drum and our drum
text: The soldiers have a drum that goes rat-a-tat, very fast, and it makes them all walk the same way like geese. Our drum is different. It is big and deep and you feel it in your chest, and it makes people want to dance, each their own way.

My sister and I copy the soldiers' drum on a hollow log and march up and down like them, very stiff, and the old men laugh until they cough. Last night a woman told us to stop. She said it was not a good week for laughing at the soldiers. I asked her why. She told me to go to bed.

tales.title: Silver brooches
text: My mother has a dress with forty silver brooches sewn on it in rows, and when she walks it chimes like rain on a kettle. The trader across the river made them, the one with the big house and the tall trees. My father traded a whole winter of furs for them.

She wears it only on great days. When I am a woman I will have a dress like that, she says, with sixty brooches. I asked her if the trader would still be here then. She took a long time to answer. Then she said someone will always be making silver.

tales.title: The night at Tippecanoe
text: Last autumn I went south with the young men to the Prophet's town on the Wabash. The Prophet, Tecumseh's brother, said we must give up the white men's goods and their whiskey and live as our grandfathers did, and that if we were strong the Americans would go back over the mountains.

Before dawn on a cold day in November we attacked the army that General Harrison had brought up to the town. I will not tell you about the fighting. When the sun came up we had lost, and the Americans burned the town. The Prophet's medicine had not stopped their bullets. Some men stopped believing in him that day. Some men only started hating the Americans more. I was one of the second.

tales.title: Main Poc's messenger
text: Main Poc is the greatest war leader of our people. He was born without fingers on one hand, and he says the spirits did that so he would know he was marked for them. He has gone over to the British at Amherstburg, and he will not take the Americans' presents, though they have offered him many.

This morning his runner came into the camp with a red belt. Fox Running, they call him. He says the British have won in the north, and that Mackinac is theirs and Detroit will be next, and that every warrior who wants to be a man should come with him. I listened all morning. Go and find him. He will tell you, too. He tells everyone.

tales.title: The man with the medal
text: Black Partridge wears a medal on his chest that the American general Wayne hung on him at Greenville, seventeen years ago, when the peace was made. He has kept faith with it all this time. He has told his young men to leave the Americans alone, and mostly they have listened.

This week they do not listen. They say the soldiers have broken their word, pouring the whiskey and the powder away. Black Partridge sat by his fire all afternoon and said nothing. Tonight, they say, he will walk into the captain's house and give the medal back. I do not know what that means for tomorrow. Nobody does. Ask him, if you can find him. He will tell you the truth, because he has never told anything else.

tales.title: A winter on credit
text: The traders give us goods in the fall on credit: powder, lead, blankets, kettles, traps, a gun if you are a good hunter. In spring we pay them back in furs. If the winter is good, you pay and have something left. If the winter is bad, you owe. And the next fall you owe more.

My father owed the old French trader at the river mouth before the Americans came. I owe the trader with the big house now. He is fair, as traders go. He makes silver that my wife loves. But when a man always owes, he is not quite free. The Americans call it trade. My father had another word for it.

tales.title: The great game
text: Last summer we played the ball game against the people from the St. Joseph River, a hundred men on each side, from noon until the sun touched the trees. The goals were half a mile apart. I broke my stick and two fingers and played on with a borrowed stick.

We won. My wife won three kettles and a blanket betting on us, and she said I could break all my fingers if it meant another blanket. We call the game the little brother of war. It teaches a man to run, to take a blow, to keep his head when everyone around him has lost theirs. This summer nobody plays. The big brother has come instead.

tales.title: The deer that waited
text: In the winter our family goes to the hunting grounds on the Kankakee, three lodges, my brothers and their wives and children. Last winter the snow was deep and the deer were few. For twelve days I hunted and brought back nothing.

On the thirteenth day I sat in the snow beside a trail at dawn and prayed and waited, and a doe walked out of the trees and stopped and looked at me, as if she had come on purpose. I thanked her before I shot. We ate. My children lived. Now some men say we should go back to the old ways, as if we had ever left them. I never left. I always thank the deer.

tales.title: It was not our people at the farm
text: In April strangers came to the farm on the South Branch and killed the two men there. The soldiers said it was Potawatomi. It was not. They were Winnebago, from the west, men none of us knew. Even the Frenchman at the farm could see it by their paint before they killed him.

But the soldiers do not care whose paint it was. To them we are all one people, the same face. Since April they look at us all the same way. A man who is looked at like an enemy every day for four months begins to wonder why he should not be one.

tales.title: The treaty at Fort Wayne
text: Three years ago at Fort Wayne the American governor, Harrison, sat with some of our chiefs and the Miami and the Delaware, and when they got up again the Americans had three million acres along the Wabash. Some of our men had touched the pen. Some had not been asked.

That is when Tecumseh began to speak in every village. He said the land belongs to all the nations together, like the air, and no chief can sell what is not his alone. I believed him. I still believe him. I have seen what happens when you let men sell the earth one piece at a time. In the end there is nowhere left to stand.

tales.title: The man with two peoples
text: William Wells came in yesterday with the Miami. He was born an American, taken by the Miami as a boy, raised as one of them. He fought beside Little Turtle against the Americans and beat them, and then he went back to the Americans and fought beside them against us.

Some men here hate him more than any soldier, because he knows our ways and uses them against us. Some men respect him, because he has never pretended to be what he is not. I do not know which I feel. I know he came to take his niece home. A man who would ride into this camp for his niece is brave, or a fool, or both.

tales.title: Fishing at the river mouth
text: At the mouth of the river where it meets the lake, the fish come up in the spring so thick you can spear them from the bank. Sturgeon as long as a man, whitefish, pike with teeth like a dog's. We build weirs of stakes and catch them by the hundred and smoke them on racks over slow fires.

The soldiers watched us the first year, and then they tried to do it themselves with nets, and caught each other more than fish. Now they buy from us, or did. I took a string of fish to the fort this spring and a soldier paid me with tobacco and a joke I did not understand. He laughed so hard I laughed too. That was before.

tales.title: The black horse
text: I have a black horse I got from the Sauk two summers ago, in trade for a gun and two blankets. He is the fastest horse on this river. The soldiers' officers have tried to buy him three times. The captain's wife looked at him the way some men look at women.

I would not sell him. A horse like that is a man's legs and his pride. This week the young men talk of what they will take from the fort when it is empty, horses and guns and kettles. I already have the best horse. I only want to keep him. That is all most men want, in the end.

tales.title: What the whiskey does
text: The whiskey the traders bring makes men into something else. I have seen a good man, a father, a hunter, drink until he beat his own wife and did not know her face. I have seen men trade a whole winter's furs for a keg and then sit in the snow with nothing.

The Prophet said give it up. Some of us did. So when the soldiers poured theirs into the river last night, half the camp was angry and half the camp was glad. Me? I was glad. But I understand the anger too. A promise is a promise, even when what was promised is poison.

tales.title: Presents from the British
text: Every summer the British at Amherstburg, down the river from Detroit, give presents to every nation that comes: blankets, kettles, guns, powder, silver, ribbons, vermilion. They call us their children and the king our father, and they feast us for days.

The Americans give presents too, at their treaties, but it is never the same. The Americans want land. The British, so far, want only friends. I am not a fool. I know the British want something too. But when a man must choose between a friend who wants nothing yet and a neighbour who wants everything, he chooses the friend. Ask Fox Running what the British promised. He has just come from them.

tales.title: Old men and young men
text: In every lodge this week the old men and the young men are arguing. The old men say, we have traded with these people for nine years, we have eaten their bread and they ours, we have children together. The young men say, they took the land on the Wabash, they burned the Prophet's town, they poured away what they promised us.

Both are right. That is the cruel thing. When everybody is right, it is the young men who decide, because they are the ones with the strength to act. I am neither old nor young. I have been sitting between them all week, with my mouth shut and my heart heavy.

tales.title: The trader's friends
text: The trader with the big house has friends among us, real friends, men who would stand between him and a war party. Topenebe of the St. Joseph River is one. His sister is married to a trader too. He has known the Kinzies for years.

Topenebe will not let them be hurt if he can help it. He has been coming and going all week, quietly, talking to the young men and to Kinzie both. If you want to see a man walking a very narrow path, find Topenebe. He is old and his steps are careful, and he has been careful all his life.

tales.title: Fire on the prairie
text: In the fall we burn the prairie. We set the fires downwind of the camp and let them run, and the grass goes up in a wall of flame higher than a lodge, and the deer and the elk come running out of it to where the hunters wait. In the spring the burned ground comes up green and sweet, and the animals come back to graze on it.

The soldiers were terrified the first time they saw it. They rang their bell and filled every bucket. Now they know. But the prairie fire is a good teacher. It says: everything burns, and everything grows back, if the roots are deep enough. I wonder how deep our roots are.

tales.title: So many fires
text: Every day more people come into the camps. From the Illinois River, from the Kankakee, from the Fox, from Milwaukee, from the Wabash. Five hundred men, they say, and their families. More fires on the prairie at night than stars.

There is not enough food for so many. The women have been out every day digging roots and the men hunting, and still the children are hungry. A hungry camp is an angry camp. The soldiers have food in their storehouse. The soldiers are leaving. You do not need a wise man to tell you what the young men are thinking.

tales.title: My cornfield
text: The cornfield is mine. My mother's mother cleared it, and her daughters have planted it, and when I die it will be my daughter's. The men hunt and fight and talk at councils. The women own the fields and the lodges, and a man who forgets that will sleep outside.

I plant in the spring when the oak leaves are the size of a mouse's ear. Corn, beans, squash, all together in hills, as the Creator taught us. This year the corn is fine and tall. And the camp is so full of strangers that I have had to set my sister's boys to guard it from hungry people every night. I have never had to do that before.

tales.title: Weaving the lodge
text: Our summer lodge is covered with mats I wove myself from cattails and bulrushes, cut in the marsh and dried and sewn with a bone needle and basswood thread. It takes a whole summer to make enough mats for a lodge. When the wind blows, the mats breathe, and the lodge is cool.

In the winter we use bark, elm or birch, which is warmer. A woman who weaves good mats is respected. A woman who weaves bad ones is talked about. I have been talked about once, when I was young and lazy. Never again. You do not want the old women talking about you.

tales.title: The soldiers' wives at the river
text: There are a few women in the fort, soldiers' wives, who come down to the river to wash. At first they were afraid of us and we laughed at them. They wear so many clothes in summer, layers and layers, that they look like onions.

Now we nod. One of them, with yellow hair, has a baby the same age as mine. We sit on the bank and let the babies look at each other, which babies like more than anything. She gave me a little mirror. I gave her a pair of moccasins for the baby. This week I have not gone down to the river. I do not know if she has.

tales.title: A woman married across the river
text: Archange, who lives across the river with her French husband Ouilmette, is one of us. She married him years ago and she keeps her house the way we keep ours, and his way too, both at once. Her children speak French to their father and our language to her and English to the soldiers.

This week her people are on one side of the river and her husband's friends on the other, and she lives in the middle. Her husband says they will stay home tomorrow. Just stay home. Find Archange if you can. She will give you something to eat, whoever you are. That is how she has always been.

tales.title: Too many mouths
text: When people come to a camp, you feed them. That is the law of the Creator and every woman knows it. So when the people came from the Wabash and the Illinois and the Fox, we fed them, until the corn of last year was gone and we started on this year's green ears.

Now I dig for roots in the marsh every day, and my daughters pick berries, and the men bring a duck or two. It is not enough. My youngest cried all night last night. I told her a story to make her sleep. When she slept I sat by the fire and thought about the soldiers' storehouse, full of flour, and their wagons, ready to carry it away.

tales.title: Ribbons on a skirt
text: I bought silk ribbon from the trader last spring, red and blue and yellow, and I have been sewing it onto my best skirt all summer, cutting it in shapes and turning the edges under, layer on layer, the way my mother taught me. The shapes come from my dreams. Nobody else has this pattern. Nobody is allowed to copy it.

When I wear it to a dance, the women will know it is mine before they see my face. That is what ribbonwork is for. The ribbon comes from the traders, from France, from England, from wherever silk is made. The pattern comes from me.

tales.title: He came home from the Wabash
text: My husband went south last fall to the Prophet's town, with a gun and new moccasins I had made him. He came home in the first snow with his arm in a sling and his eyes different. He did not speak for many days.

He has healed now, mostly. He can hunt again. But at night he talks in his sleep, and once he woke and did not know where he was and reached for his gun. This week the young men are talking war again, and he sits with them. I want to tell him he has done enough. I do not. A woman learns when a man cannot hear her.

tales.title: The plants by the marsh
text: My grandmother taught me the plants: which root eases a fever, which leaf to put on a burn, which bark makes a tea for a cough. The soldiers' young doctor came to watch me gathering once and asked through the interpreter what each one was for. He wrote it all down in a little book.

I asked him why he wanted to know. He said his medicines came from very far away and often did not work. I liked him for saying so. Most of them think nothing that grows here can be any good. That doctor will learn this country, if anyone gives him time.

tales.title: Sugar in birch bark
text: I make the sugar every spring. I tap the maples, catch the sap in bark pans, and boil it in a brass kettle I bought from the trader, all day and all night, until it is thick enough to beat into grains. Then I pack it in birch bark boxes called mokuks, sewn with root and scratched with pictures on the lid.

The trader buys my sugar. His family puts it on everything. His children love it. Last spring his boy came running to me with his hand out, the oldest boy, John. I gave him a piece and he said thank you in our language, very badly. I laughed. He laughed. That was a good day.

tales.title: My daughter and the Frenchman
text: My daughter is going to marry a Frenchman who trades on the Des Plaines. He came to my lodge and sat with my husband and gave presents, as is right, and asked for her properly. He speaks our language well enough. He is not a bad man.

But I am afraid for her. When a woman marries a trader, she becomes the bridge between his people and ours. Everyone walks across her. In a good year, it makes her strong. In a year like this one, a bridge is the first thing that burns.

tales.title: For a child
text: Two winters ago I lost my son to the coughing sickness. He was four. For a year I wore my hair loose and my face unpainted, and I kept a bundle with his things in it, his little moccasins and his toy bow, and I fed it at every meal as if he were still with us. At the end of the year we gave a feast and gave his things away and let him go on his road.

I tell you this because the soldiers' wife lost her baby in the spring, the captain's wife, and I saw her walking alone on the beach. I wanted to tell her how we do it, how there is a year for grief and then a feast. I did not have the words. I wish I had.

tales.title: The first trader at the river
text: When I was a young man the first trader to live at the river mouth was a Black man named Point du Sable. He was French in his speech and from the south, from the islands some said. He married a woman of our people, Kitihawa, and built a big house on the north bank, where the trader Kinzie lives now.

He was a good man. He had cattle and horses and a mill, and he traded fair. When he left, about twelve summers ago, he sold everything and went down the Illinois River and we never saw him again. People forget him now. I do not. He was the first one who came here to live with us instead of to take from us.

tales.title: When I was young
text: When I was very young, the French were our fathers, and then the English came and the French went away. My father fought for the great war chief Pontiac, who tried to drive the English out. That was fifty summers ago. The English won, and then a few years later they made peace and gave us presents.

Then the Americans fought the English and won, and the English went over the river into Canada, and the Americans came. Every few summers a new father. I am old. I have learned that the fathers change but the land stays the same. It was here before all of them. It will be here after.

tales.title: Stories wait for the snow
text: The old stories, the true ones, about how the world was made and how the animals got their ways, we tell only in the winter, when there is snow on the ground. That is how my grandmother taught me. In the summer the spirits are awake and listening, and it is not polite to talk about them behind their backs.

So I will not tell you one of those. But I will tell you a story of my own life, which I may tell in any season. When I was born, the French were here. Then the English. Now the Americans. And every one of them told us, this land is ours now. As if the land had ever listened to anyone.

tales.title: The day the soldiers came
text: Nine summers ago, a ship came across the lake and soldiers came marching in along the shore, and they walked up to the high ground by the bend of the river and started cutting trees. They cut so many trees. My people stood on the bank and watched them dig and build, and we said to each other, what are they afraid of, that they build such walls?

Their captain, Whistler, was a fair man. He paid for the logs and let us trade at his gate. But I remember thinking that a people who build a wall around themselves in someone else's country must believe they will need it. Now, nine summers later, they are leaving their wall. I wonder if they ever needed it, or if the wall was what made them need it.

tales.title: The spotted sickness
text: When I was a boy the spotted sickness came through the villages. It came with the traders' goods, people said, in blankets and cloth. My mother died of it, and two of my sisters, and so many others that there were not enough people left to bury them properly.

I lived. I have the marks on my face still, here, and here. The sickness does not care if you are brave, or wise, or kind. It is the one enemy every nation fears the same. When I hear the young men talk of war, I think: there are worse things than soldiers. I have seen them.

tales.title: What an old man knows
text: Young men think that courage is running at the enemy. Old men know that courage is sitting still when every part of you wants to run. Tonight I am going to sit by the fire and not speak and not sleep, and listen to the young men talk, and try to keep my face calm.

Tomorrow will come whether I sleep or not. The soldiers will march, and the young men will do what they have decided, and the old men will not be able to stop them. But someone must sit still and remember everything. That is the old man's job. Somebody has to tell the story afterwards.

tales.title: Little Turtle is gone
text: A month ago our great chief Little Turtle died at Fort Wayne, of the gout and old age, in the house of his son-in-law, William Wells. He was the one who beat two American armies, long ago, and then made peace and kept it. He went to see the President in Philadelphia and they made him a sword.

Wells loved him like a father. When he buried him, the Americans gave him a soldier's funeral, with guns firing. Now Wells has ridden here with us to bring his niece home. He has not spoken of Little Turtle once on the road. That is how I know how much it hurts him.

tales.title: Thirty Miami on the road
text: We rode from Fort Wayne, about thirty of us with Captain Wells. We were sent to bring the soldiers and their families safely home along the lake. That is our job. It is a strange job, walking between the soldiers and the Potawatomi, with old friends on both sides.

The Potawatomi here look at us with hard eyes. Some of them are our cousins. Some of them think we have become the Americans' dogs. I do not think about that. I think about the road, and the wagons, and the women and children, and how to get them home. One thing at a time. That is how you get through a hard road.

tales.title: Between two nations
text: My grandfather fought the Americans with Little Turtle and won. My father made peace with them at Greenville. I ride with an American now, Wells, who is also a Miami, who was once an American, who is now both. If that confuses you, imagine how it feels to be us.

The Miami are tired of war. We have lost too many men, too many villages, too much land. Some of our young men went to Tecumseh. Most stayed home. We want to plant our corn and raise our children. Is that so much to want? Tomorrow we will find out.

tales.title: The horses are tired
text: Our horses are tired from the road and there is not enough grass near the fort for them, with so many Potawatomi horses already grazing every blade. I have been taking them out to the prairie at dawn, further each day, with two others to watch.

Out there you can see how many lodges there are now. More every morning. I counted the smoke one dawn and stopped at three hundred. I came back and told Captain Wells. He only nodded. He knew. He has known since the day we arrived.

tales.title: My mother
text: My mother is over there. She is making the fire. She sings when she works.
I had a bad dream. My mother picked me up. She smells like smoke and corn. Now I am not scared. You can stay. You can listen to my mother sing.

tales.title: The dog
text: There is a dog. He is brown. He licked my face. It tickled.
I gave him my corn cake. All of it. Then I had none. My sister gave me some of hers. The dog wants that too. No, dog.

tales.title: Splash
text: The water by the river is cold. I put my feet in. Splash, splash. A fish swam by my toes.
I tried to catch it. It went away. Fish are very fast. When I am big I will catch a fish. A big one. Bigger than you.

tales.title: The bird
text: A bird sat on a branch. It was red. It said tweet, tweet. Then it flew up, up, up.
I flapped my arms. I did not fly. My brother laughed. I will try again tomorrow. Birds can do it. I am bigger than a bird.

tales.title: The moon
text: At night there is a moon. It is round and white. It follows me when I walk.
I said hello moon. The moon did not say anything. My grandmother says the moon is shy. She says if I am very quiet, it will come closer. I am being very quiet.

tales.title: No midwife at the end of the world
text: There is no midwife here. Not one, between this fort and Fort Wayne. When a woman's time comes she has the doctor, who is a boy, and the other wives, who do their best, and the Potawatomi women across the river, who know more than all of us together.

In May the captain's wife lost her first child, a son born dead. Rebekah Heald is only twenty-two and she rode all the way here from Kentucky on horseback to be married at the edge of the map. She does not speak of the baby. She rides out every afternoon instead, very fast, along the shore. Find her if you like. Do not mention it. Ask her about her horse.

tales.title: The washing on the river
text: I do the washing for six of the soldiers and my own family. That is a fire, a kettle, a tub, a paddle, and a whole morning on my knees at the river bank with lye soap that takes the skin off your hands.

The Potawatomi women come down to the same bank with their children, and we have learned to nod to each other, and then to talk with our hands, and then, a few words. One of them showed me how to bleach linen in the sun on the grass. One of them laughed at my bonnet until she cried. This week they did not come down to the river. I washed alone. That is how I knew.

tales.title: The night we ran into the fort
text: In April, when word came of the killings at Lee's farm, every family in the settlement left their houses in the dark. Nobody took anything but the children and a blanket. I carried my youngest on my hip and dragged the other by the hand, and the soldiers held the gate open with lanterns until the last of us was in.

We have lived in the fort ever since. Four months, crowded into the officers' quarters and the storerooms with the soldiers' wives. My own house is just over there, a few hundred yards, with the door shut and the garden gone to weeds. I can see it from the walls. I will not see it again after tomorrow.

tales.title: What will fit in a wagon
text: The captain says each family may take what will fit in the wagons, and the wagons are already full of the sick and the children. So I have been deciding all day what to leave.

My mother's pewter. My husband's good coat. The cradle. A Bible with all our names written in the front, back to my grandfather. I put the Bible in my apron pocket in the end, and the cradle stays. The little one is too big for it anyway, though I told myself she was not. A woman packs the past on a day like this. The past is heavier than you think.

tales.title: Mrs. Kinzie's boat
text: The Kinzies will not march in the column tomorrow. Mrs. Kinzie and the children will go by water, in their own boat, with the boatmen and the nurse, and meet us down the lake. Mr. Kinzie will walk with the soldiers, because he says he will not be seen to hide.

Mrs. Kinzie was taken herself as a girl, they say, carried off from Pennsylvania by the Senecas and raised among them, and she knows the people in the camps better than any officer here. She has said nothing about tomorrow, only gone on packing in that quiet way of hers. Find her and ask her. She will tell you more with one look than the captain tells in a speech.

tales.title: The lieutenant's young wife
text: Margaret Helm is seventeen and she married the lieutenant last year, and she is the merriest creature in this whole sad fort. She is Mrs. Kinzie's daughter by her first husband, a British officer, so her late father wore the King's coat and her husband wears the President's.

She can ride, and she can shoot, and she has told us all she is not afraid of anything. I think it is mostly true. She is going to ride with the column tomorrow instead of going in her mother's boat, because she will not leave her husband. Find her, and ask her why. She will laugh and tell you, as if it were the simplest thing in the world.

tales.title: Corn in hills
text: When I first came here I planted corn the way my father did in Ohio, in straight rows, and the Potawatomi women laughed at me. They showed me how they do it: a hill of earth, three or four kernels, beans to climb the stalk, and squash below to keep the weeds down. Three sisters, they called it, through the interpreter.

My corn was better that year than it had ever been. I tried to thank the woman who showed me and she shrugged, as if anyone could have known that. I wonder whose corn will feed whose children this winter. I would like to think it will be hers.

tales.title: Bread, pork and nothing
text: You would think a fort would eat well. You would be wrong. Salt pork, hard bread, beans, and when the boats are late, nothing at all. The fresh meat is whatever the hunters bring, and the hunters this summer have stopped bringing it.

Mr. Kinzie's people have the best table in the place, with venison and wild duck and fish from the lake, and maple sugar in a bark box that they put on everything. Last Christmas Mrs. Kinzie sent us a whole wild turkey. I have never forgotten it. That is the thing about a small place. One kindness is enough to keep you warm all year.

tales.title: A sister in Kentucky
text: My sister writes from Kentucky that she cannot imagine how I live. No church, no shop, no doctor, no neighbours but soldiers and savages, she says. I wrote back and told her she has the neighbours wrong.

The woman across the river who brings us fish has three children and a husband who is away hunting half the year, just like me. Her baby cut his first tooth the same week as mine. We do not speak each other's language and we both know what a tooth does to a night's sleep. That is not a savage. That is a neighbour. My sister has not written back.

tales.title: The captain's wife rides
text: Rebekah Heald came here in 1811 on horseback, all the way from Louisville, a bride of twenty, with her husband and her servant Cicely and Cicely's baby. She rode the whole way. The officers' wives in Detroit, they say, would have gone by boat and been carried ashore.

She is the niece of Captain Wells, the scout, and she rides like him, low on the horse's neck, fast. The officers say she is a fine shot as well. Tomorrow she rides with the column. I have seen her checking her saddle girth twice an hour all afternoon. She is not as calm as she looks.

tales.title: A baby born in the fort
text: Susan Simmons has a baby girl not two months old, and a boy of six, David, who follows the soldiers everywhere and salutes the captain. Her husband is a private. She is from Pennsylvania and she says the winters here are no worse than home, which is how you know she is a liar and a brave one.

She has wrapped the baby in so many shawls for the march that the child looks like a loaf of bread. I asked her if she was afraid. She said a woman with a baby does not have time to be afraid, and that is the truest thing anyone has said to me all week. Go and see her. The baby is very pretty, under all those shawls.

tales.title: Singing at night
text: The voyageurs at the Kinzie house sing in the evenings, songs from Canada about a girl and a river and a rose. I do not understand the words, but I hear them across the water every night, and they make the fort feel less alone.

This week they have stopped singing. I asked one of them why and he said it was not a week for songs. Then he laughed and sang one line, very low, and stopped. I do not know what the line meant. I asked the interpreter later and he said it was something about going home.

tales.title: Silver for the trade
text: Mr. Kinzie was a silversmith before he was a trader, and he still makes the silver himself: brooches, ear-bobs, arm bands, crosses, little round gorgets with holes for the thread. The Potawatomi wear it sewn on their clothes in rows, so that a man in his best coat shines like a lake in the sun.

That is how Kinzie built the trade here. Not with guns or whiskey, though he sells those too, but with silver that people wanted to wear. He knows every chief's name and every chief's wife's name, and the names of their children. If you want to understand Chicago, find him. He is the town, more than the fort is.

tales.title: The quarrel at the gate
text: Two months ago, at sunset on the seventeenth of June, Mr. Kinzie and the government interpreter, Jean Lalime, met just outside the gate as it was being shut. Words were said. Nobody agrees what they were about. Some say the trade, some say an old grudge, some say Lalime had been writing letters to Fort Wayne about Kinzie.

They fought, and when it was over Kinzie had a wound in his neck and Lalime lay dead. A friend took Kinzie off to Milwaukee that night, until it was safe to come back. Lalime is buried in front of the Kinzie house, inside a little picket fence, where Kinzie sees the grave every morning from his porch. I do not know how a man drinks his coffee looking at that.

tales.title: The portage in a wet spring
text: The Chicago portage is the gate of the whole West. Paddle up the South Branch, cross the mud at Mud Lake, and you are in the Des Plaines and on your way to the Illinois and the Mississippi. In a wet spring you can float a canoe the whole way. In a dry summer you carry everything on your back through mud to your knees.

Antoine Ouilmette has done that carrying for Mr. Kinzie for years. Packs of ninety pounds, two at a time, on a strap across his forehead. He says the mosquitoes on the portage are the size of sparrows. He is exaggerating, but not by as much as you would hope. Find him and ask him to show you his strap.

tales.title: Hardscrabble
text: Lee's farm on the South Branch fed this fort. Wheat, cattle, hogs, the first proper farm on this river. People call it Hardscrabble, because that is what it is: a hard scrabble on wet land.

Since April it has stood empty. The two men who worked it are buried, the cattle are scattered, and the fields have gone to grass and wild flowers. Charles Lee rode out once in July with a guard of soldiers and came back without a word. They say he wants to sell. I do not know who would buy. Ask him yourself. He is a proud man, and it may do him good to talk.

tales.title: An old soldier's house
text: Thomas Burns served his time in this same fort and then stayed, and built a house on the north bank, and married the widow Cooper with all her children. He says a soldier who finishes his five years here has two choices: go home and tell lies about the West, or stay and find out which of the lies are true.

He found out. He grew corn and kept a cow and made friends among the camps. Now he is our sergeant of militia, and his house stands empty across the river with the cow inside it. He says the cow is the only one of us with any sense.

tales.title: The French on the north bank
text: There were Frenchmen here before there was a fort, before there was a United States in this country at all. Louis Fettle lives in one of the old log houses on the north bank with his Indian wife. He was here when the soldiers came in 1803 to build the fort, and he watched them cut the logs and laughed at how they did it.

The French came to trade, and they stayed, and they married into the families of the camps, and their children speak three languages before they can walk. When the Americans talk about the frontier, the French smile. To them it is not a frontier. It is home, and it has been for a hundred years.

tales.title: The government store
text: Across from the fort stands the government's trading house, the factory. The idea was that the government would sell goods to the Potawatomi at a fair price, cheaper than the British traders, and so win their friendship. Mr. Irwin, the factor, ran it for three years, and in all that time he complained that the Indians liked Kinzie's goods better than his.

He left in July and gave the keys to Doctor Van Voorhis. Now the store is being emptied out to the camps, as the captain promised, bolts of cloth, kettles, blankets, paint. The people take them and look at the fort and do not say thank you. You cannot buy a friend in a week with what you would not sell him for three years.

tales.title: The clerk who speaks to everyone
text: Jean Baptiste Chandonnai is Mr. Kinzie's clerk, and he is the only man in Chicago who is welcome in every house and every lodge. He is French and Potawatomi both, and young, and he moves between the trading house and the camps like a fish between rocks.

He keeps the books, and he translates, and he carries messages. This week he has been carrying a great many messages. Everyone wants to know what everyone else is thinking, and he is the only one who can ask. If you find him, he will greet you kindly. He is very good at greeting people kindly and telling them nothing.

tales.title: The young man who brought the war
text: Pierre Le Clerc lives a few yards from the fort and works for Mr. Kinzie. He is young and quick and French and Indian, and they say it was he who first brought word to Chicago in July that the war had begun.

He will march with the soldiers tomorrow, he says, and fight for them if it comes to that. Some of the officers do not trust him, because he has cousins in the camps. I think a man with cousins on both sides is the one most worth trusting, because he has the most to lose either way. Find Peresh. Ask him what his cousins say.

tales.title: A quart of corn and two ounces of tallow
text: An engagé of Mr. Kinzie gets a quart of lyed corn a day and two ounces of tallow to cook it with, and that is all, and that is enough. You boil the corn in lye until the skins come off, wash it, boil it again, and eat it with the fat. Every day. All winter.

In the fall we go out to the wintering grounds with the trade goods, and in spring we come back with the packs of furs, beaver and muskrat and otter, and then we sing and drink and fight and spend everything, and in the fall we go out again. That is a voyageur's life. It is a good life. It is the only one I know.

tales.title: Songs for the oars
text: We sing because a song keeps the paddles together. Forty strokes a minute, all day, from dawn until dark, and a good song can get you another league before the steersman lets you rest. The bowman starts it, the rest answer.

There is one about a girl who drops her ring in the river, and one about a duck, and one about a soldier who comes home to find his sweetheart married. The Americans think they are all happy songs because we sing them so loud. Most of them are sad. That is why we sing them loud.

tales.title: A winter on the Kankakee
text: Last winter I was sent with the goods to a wintering post on the Kankakee River, two of us and a Potawatomi family who traded with us. For four months I saw no other white face. The snow came up to the roof of our hut and the wolves sat in a ring around it at night and sang.

The family took us in when our flour ran out. The old woman gave me a pair of moccasins lined with rabbit fur, and I wore them until they fell to pieces. When I came back to Chicago in the spring I had forgotten how to talk to Americans. I have not entirely remembered.

tales.title: The family boat
text: Tomorrow I am at the oars of the Kinzie boat. We will take the family and the nurse and the servants down the river and out the mouth, and wait there for the column to pass, and then follow along the shore.

My friend who rows with me was born on the Saint Lawrence and his father was a voyageur before him. He says a boat is the safest place in a storm and the worst place in a battle, because you cannot hide in it and you cannot run. I told him there will be no battle. He looked at me the way you look at a child who has said something sweet and foolish.

meet.name: A second Kinzie engagé, name not recorded

tales.title: Beaver in the old days
text: The old men say that when the French first came here, the beaver were so thick on the rivers you could walk across their dams. Then the trade began, and every man wanted a beaver hat, from Paris to New York, and every beaver in the country went to make them.

Now we take muskrat mostly, and deer hides, and raccoon. The beaver are far off to the north and west. The trade follows them like a wolf follows a herd. One day there will be none left anywhere, and then what will the traders do? Farm, I suppose. Heaven help them.

tales.title: The lodging house for the Frenchmen
text: Mr. Kinzie keeps a lodging house beside his own for us, his hired men. Bunks, a fire, a table, a fiddle on the wall that nobody can play properly. In the evening we sit there and smoke and argue about which of us has the worst back.

Tonight nobody is arguing. Everybody is mending something, or sharpening something, or packing something. Old Baptiste, who is the best storyteller among us, started a story about a werewolf in Quebec and stopped halfway through, and nobody asked him to finish. That never happens.

tales.title: Cicely's road from Louisville
text: The captain's household came up from Louisville last year, on horseback, a month on the road through the woods. Mrs. Heald rode, and the captain rode, and Cicely rode with her baby boy held in front of her. Cicely is enslaved to the Healds. The Ordinance says there shall be no slavery in this country; they brought her anyway, and nobody here has said a word.

She runs the captain's quarters. She cooks, she mends, she knows the captain's moods before he does. She has a son and no other family within a thousand miles. If you speak to her, call her by her name. Ask about her boy. That is the one subject on which she will smile for you.

tales.title: The man in the bow
text: Black Jim works for the Kinzies. Whether he is free or held, nobody here has ever written down, and he does not say. He is strong and quiet and he does the heavy work of the house, the wood, the water, the boats.

Tomorrow he will be in the bow of the Kinzie boat with the family. I saw him this evening checking the boat over plank by plank, and he set an axe under the bow seat where he could reach it. When he saw me looking he only nodded. A man who checks his boat that carefully is not expecting a pleasant trip.

tales.title: The children's nurse
text: Josette LaFramboise is nurse to the Kinzie children. She is young, French and Ottawa, from a family of traders up the lake, and she speaks to the children in three languages so that they answer in whichever one they feel like.

She will be in the boat tomorrow with the little ones. She has sewn pockets inside the children's clothes and filled them with dried corn and maple sugar, in case. She did not tell anyone she was doing it. I found out because the baby was chewing on his pocket. Find Josette and ask her about the pockets. She will say she has no idea what you mean.

tales.title: Nobody writes down my name
text: I work in the Kinzie house. I fetch, I carry, I scrub, I mind the fire. When the gentlemen write their letters they will say Mr. Kinzie and his family and two servants. That is me. One of the two servants.

But I am a person all the same, and I have my own fears tonight, and my own prayers. I have friends in the camps and friends in the fort. I know how the master takes his tea and how the mistress hides her worry. If anybody ever asks who was in that boat, I hope somebody remembers there were two of us, and that we were brave.

tales.title: The letter from Detroit
text: Five days ago a chief called Winnemeg walked in at the gate with a letter from General Hull, and the whole post went quiet. We are to leave the fort. Give up Fort Dearborn, hand out the goods, and march for Fort Wayne. Some of the old hands said it plain: the safest walls between here and Detroit are the ones we are standing behind.

Winnemeg told Mr. Kinzie we should go at once, before the camps fill, or else stay and hold the place. We did neither. We waited, and every day more lodges went up on the prairie. If you want to know what he truly thinks, find him. He came a long way to carry bad news, and he does not look like a man who enjoyed it.

tales.title: The night the river tasted of grog
text: Last night we carried the barrels out of the sally port in the dark and stove in their heads at the river's edge. Every drop of the post's whiskey went into the Chicago River. The captain will not hand liquor to men who may be at our backs on the march, and I cannot fault him for that.

But you could smell it on the water this morning, and the men from the camps smelled it too. They came down to the bank and stood looking at the river as if it had been robbed. Then we heard the powder and the spare muskets went down the well. They had been promised those goods. A promise broken in the dark is worse than one refused in daylight. I would not want to be the man who explains it to them.

tales.title: A gill a day
text: Ensign Ronan signed an order last November that each man was to have his gill of whiskey. One gill, mind, measured out by the sergeant with a face like a church deacon. The ensign is the youngest officer in the fort, not long out of West Point, and some of the men laughed at him behind his back for being so careful with his signature.

I stopped laughing when I saw him at drill. He is earnest. He reads his manual by candle and he knows every man's name. If we have to fight our way down the shore, I would rather have a boy who reads the book than a man who has forgotten it. Go and find him if you like. He will tell you he is ready, and he will mean it.

tales.title: Five years for five dollars
text: I put my mark on the paper for five years and five dollars a month, and I was told I would see the country. I have seen it. I have seen a sandbar, a river the colour of tea, and a prairie so wide that a man walking toward you takes an hour to arrive.

The pay comes late when it comes at all. We grow our own corn and cabbages in the garden by the river, and we cut our own firewood, and in winter we break the ice for water. A soldier here is half a farmer and half a carpenter, and he is a soldier only when the drum says so. Now the drum says march. I find I do not want to leave the cabbages.

tales.title: The fifer's tunes
text: Listen at dawn tomorrow and you will hear George Burnett's fife before you hear the birds. He has been on the rolls since 1806 and he can play every call the army ever wrote, and a few it never did. He plays reveille as if he is angry at the sun for being late.

In the winter, when the snow comes up to the pickets and there is nothing to do but mend boots, he plays jigs in the barracks and the men dance with each other because there is nobody else to dance with. I have seen a sergeant waltz a corporal round the stove. If you want to hear him, ask nicely. He pretends to be shy and then plays until you beg him to stop.

tales.title: The drums tell the day
text: Everything here runs to the drum. The drum wakes you, the drum calls you to roll, the drum sends you to dinner and to bed. John Hamilton has beaten it since 1808, and Hugh McPherson beats the other one. Between them they have more say over my life than the President.

John told me once that a drummer learns to read a man's face on the parade, because he sees the whole company at once while every other man sees only the back of the head in front. He says this week the faces have changed. Men look at the gate, and then at the lodges, and then at the lake. He keeps his beat steady anyway. He says that is what a drum is for.
